questions.text: Q1. Which seventeenth-century French philosopher, mathematician, and biologist is credited with establishing the anthropocentric approach to understanding natural phenomena as mentioned in Unit IX of NCERT?
questions.solution: According to Unit IX introduction (NCERT Page 1), Rene Descartes, the seventeenth-century French philosopher, mathematician and biologist, directed natural sciences toward an anthropocentric approach for human comfort and welfare.

questions.text: Q2. In which year was Herbert Boyer born, and where was he brought up?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 2 states: 'Herbert Boyer was born in 1936 and brought up in a corner of western Pennsylvania where railroads and mines were the destiny of most young men.'

questions.text: Q3. Herbert Boyer completed his graduate work at the University of Pittsburgh in 1963, followed by three years of post-graduate studies at which prestigious university?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 2 mentions: 'He completed graduate work at the University of Pittsburgh, in 1963, followed by three years of post-graduate studies at Yale.'

questions.text: Q4. In 1969, Herbert Boyer observed that restriction enzymes of E. coli cut DNA strands in a particular fashion, producing:
questions.solution: NCERT Page 2 states: 'Boyer observed that these enzymes have the capability of cutting DNA strands in a particular fashion, which left what has became known as ‘sticky ends’ on the strands.'

questions.text: Q5. Stanley Cohen was studying small autonomous ringlets of DNA called plasmids at which university?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 2: 'Stanley Cohen was a Stanford scientist who had been studying small ringlets of DNA called plasmids which float freely in bacterial cytoplasm.'

questions.text: Q6. Where did Herbert Boyer and Stanley Cohen hold the historic discussion that laid the foundation for recombinant DNA technology?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 2 states: 'This discovery, in turn, led to a rich and rewarding conversation in Hawaii with a Stanford scientist named Stanley Cohen.'

questions.text: Q7. In traditional sense, processes like making curd, bread, or wine are considered forms of biotechnology because:
options: They use live organisms or enzymes from organisms to produce products useful to humans
questions.solution: NCERT Page 3: 'Biotechnology deals with techniques of using live organisms or enzymes from organisms to produce products and processes useful to humans. In this sense, making curd, bread or wine... could also be thought as a form of biotechnology.'

questions.text: Q8. Which of the following processes is NOT included under the modern scope of biotechnology according to NCERT?
options: In vitro fertilisation leading to a 'test-tube' baby
Developing a DNA vaccine or correcting a defective gene
questions.solution: NCERT Page 3 lists IVF, gene synthesis, DNA vaccines, and gene therapy under biotechnology. Petroleum refining is a non-biological physical separation process.

questions.text: Q9. The European Federation of Biotechnology (EFB) defines biotechnology as:
options: 'The alteration of genetic material in microbes for industrial chemical processes'
'The integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof, and molecular analogues for products and services'
'The cultivation of genetically modified organisms exclusively in bioreactors'
'The manufacturing of antibiotics using eukaryotic continuous culture systems'
questions.solution: NCERT Page 3: The definition given by EFB is: 'The integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof, and molecular analogues for products and services'.

questions.text: Q10. What are the two core techniques that enabled the birth of modern biotechnology?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 3-4 lists the two core techniques: (i) Genetic engineering, and (ii) Bioprocess engineering.

questions.text: Q11. Maintenance of a sterile (microbial contamination-free) ambience in chemical engineering processes is essential for:
questions.solution: NCERT Page 4: 'Bioprocess engineering: Maintenance of sterile (microbial contamination-free) ambience in chemical engineering processes to enable growth of only the desired microbe/eukaryotic cell in large quantities...'

questions.text: Q12. What is the primary evolutionary advantage of sexual reproduction over asexual reproduction highlighted in NCERT Chapter 9?
options: Preserves exact genetic information without any modification
Provides opportunities for variations and unique genetic combinations
questions.solution: NCERT Page 4: 'The former [sexual reproduction] provides opportunities for variations and formulation of unique combinations of genetic setup, some of which may be beneficial...'

questions.text: Q13. What is the major limitation of traditional hybridisation procedures used in plant and animal breeding?
options: It is unable to introduce any genetic variation
It very often leads to inclusion and multiplication of undesirable genes along with desired genes
It produces sterile progeny in all generations
questions.solution: NCERT Page 4: 'Traditional hybridisation procedures used in plant and animal breeding, very often lead to inclusion and multiplication of undesirable genes along with the desired genes.'

questions.text: Q14. How does genetic engineering overcome the limitations of traditional hybridization breeding?
options: By completely eliminating sexual reproduction in organisms
By allowing isolation and introduction of only desired genes without undesirable genes
By multiplying all genes present in the donor genome randomly
questions.solution: NCERT Page 4: 'The techniques of genetic engineering... allows us to isolate and introduce only one or a set of desirable genes without introducing undesirable genes into the target organism.'

questions.text: Q15. What is the most likely fate of an alien piece of DNA transferred into an organism without being integrated into a chromosome?
options: It would not be able to multiply itself in the progeny cells of the organism
questions.solution: NCERT Page 4: 'Most likely, this piece of DNA would not be able to multiply itself in the progeny cells of the organism. But, when it gets integrated into the genome of the recipient, it may multiply...'

questions.text: Q16. The specific DNA sequence responsible for initiating replication in a chromosome is termed as:
questions.solution: NCERT Page 4: 'In a chromosome there is a specific DNA sequence called the origin of replication, which is responsible for initiating replication.'

questions.text: Q17. The process of making multiple identical copies of any template DNA is known as:
questions.solution: NCERT Page 4: 'This can also be called as cloning or making multiple identical copies of any template DNA.'

questions.text: Q18. In which year was the first artificial recombinant DNA molecule constructed by Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 4: 'Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer accomplished this in 1972 by isolating the antibiotic resistance gene by cutting out a piece of DNA from a plasmid...'

questions.text: Q19. The first recombinant DNA molecule was constructed by linking an antibiotic resistance gene with the native plasmid of which bacterium?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 4 explicitly states: 'linking a gene encoding antibiotic resistance with a native plasmid (autonomously replicating circular extra-chromosomal DNA) of Salmonella typhimurium.'

questions.text: Q20. A plasmid is best defined biologically as:
questions.solution: NCERT Page 4 defines plasmid as: 'autonomously replicating circular extra-chromosomal DNA'.

questions.text: Q21. Which enzyme made possible the linking of the antibiotic resistance gene with the plasmid vector in the 1972 breakthrough experiment?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'The linking of antibiotic resistance gene with the plasmid vector became possible with the enzyme DNA ligase, which acts on cut DNA molecules and joins their ends.'

questions.text: Q22. When the first recombinant DNA created in vitro was transferred into E. coli, it multiplied using which host enzyme?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'When this DNA is transferred into Escherichia coli... it could replicate using the new host’s DNA polymerase enzyme and make multiple copies.'

questions.text: Q23. According to NCERT, how many basic steps are involved in genetically modifying an organism?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5 lists three basic steps: (i) identification of DNA with desirable genes, (ii) introduction into host, (iii) maintenance in host and transfer to progeny.

questions.text: Q24. Which of the following represents the correct sequence of the three basic steps in genetically modifying an organism?
options: Introduction into host → Identification of DNA → Maintenance and transfer
Identification of DNA with desirable genes → Introduction of identified DNA into host → Maintenance and transfer to progeny
Maintenance in host → Transfer to progeny → Identification of DNA
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5 clearly outlines: (i) Identification, (ii) Introduction, and (iii) Maintenance and transfer to progeny.

questions.text: Q25. In recombinant DNA technology, the vehicle used to deliver an alien piece of DNA into the host organism is called a:
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'These plasmid DNA act as vectors to transfer the piece of DNA attached to it... In the same way, a plasmid can be used as vector to deliver an alien piece of DNA into the host organism.'

questions.text: Q26. NCERT compares the function of a plasmid vector delivering DNA to a host cell with which biological analogy?
options: Mosquito transferring malarial parasite into the human body
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'You probably know that mosquito acts as an insect vector to transfer the malarial parasite into human body. In the same way, a plasmid can be used as vector to deliver an alien piece of DNA...'

questions.text: Q27. Which of the following is NOT listed as a key tool of recombinant DNA technology in Section 9.2 of NCERT?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'recombinant DNA technology can be accomplished only if we have the key tools, i.e., restriction enzymes, polymerase enzymes, ligases, vectors and the host organism.'

questions.text: Q28. The ability to multiply copies of an antibiotic resistance gene in E. coli is referred to as:
options: Cloning of antibiotic resistance gene in E. coli
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'The ability to multiply copies of antibiotic resistance gene in E. coli was called cloning of antibiotic resistance gene in E. coli.'

questions.text:
Q29. Read the following statements:
Statement I: Asexual reproduction preserves genetic information.
Statement II: Sexual reproduction permits genetic variation.
Choose the correct option:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution: NCERT Page 4 explicitly states: 'Asexual reproduction preserves the genetic information, while sexual reproduction permits variation.' Both statements are correct.

questions.text:
Q30. Consider the following statements regarding Cohen and Boyer's experiment:
(A) It was performed in 1972.
(B) Antibiotic resistance gene was linked with native plasmid of E. coli.
(C) DNA ligase joined the cut ends.
(D) The recombinant plasmid was transferred to Salmonella.
Which of the above statements are CORRECT?
questions.solution: (B) is incorrect because the native plasmid was from Salmonella typhimurium. (D) is incorrect because recombinant DNA was transferred into E. coli. Hence, only (A) and (C) are correct.

questions.text: Q31. Which of the following products is manufactured on a large scale using bioprocess engineering?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 4: '...manufacture of biotechnological products like antibiotics, vaccines, enzymes, etc.'

questions.text: Q32. Why is an alien piece of DNA linked specifically with the origin of replication for cloning?
options: Because ori sequence initiates replication, allowing the alien DNA to multiply in the host
questions.solution: NCERT Page 4: 'In a chromosome there is a specific DNA sequence called the origin of replication, which is responsible for initiating replication. Thus, an alien DNA is linked with the origin of replication, so that, this alien piece of DNA can replicate...'

questions.text: Q33. The technique that allows alteration of the chemistry of genetic material (DNA and RNA) is known as:
questions.solution: NCERT Page 3: 'Genetic engineering : Techniques to alter the chemistry of genetic material (DNA and RNA), to introduce these into host organisms and thus change the phenotype...'

questions.text: Q34. Salmonella typhimurium is closely related to which commonly used host bacterium?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'When this DNA is transferred into Escherichia coli, a bacterium closely related to Salmonella...'

questions.text: Q35. What term is used in NCERT to describe the cut piece of DNA carrying desirable traits that is selected for transfer into a vector?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 4-5 refers to the target DNA as 'alien piece of DNA' or 'gene of interest'.

questions.text: Q36. In the year 1963, two enzymes responsible for restricting the growth of bacteriophage in Escherichia coli were isolated. What were the specific actions of these two enzymes?
options: One added methyl groups to DNA, while the other cut DNA
One synthesized RNA, while the other degraded proteins
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'In the year 1963, the two enzymes responsible for restricting the growth of bacteriophage in Escherichia coli were isolated. One of these added methyl groups to DNA, while the other cut DNA.'

questions.text: Q37. The enzyme isolated in 1963 that cut bacteriophage DNA was called a:
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'One of these added methyl groups to DNA, while the other cut DNA. The later was called restriction endonuclease.'

questions.text: Q38. Which was the FIRST restriction endonuclease to be isolated and characterized whose functioning depended on a specific DNA nucleotide sequence?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'The first restriction endonuclease–Hind II, whose functioning depended on a specific DNA nucleotide sequence was isolated and characterised five years later.'

questions.text: Q39. Hind II was isolated how many years after the initial 1963 discovery of restriction enzymes?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'The first restriction endonuclease–Hind II... was isolated and characterised five years later (i.e. in 1968)'.

questions.text: Q40. The specific recognition sequence recognized and cut by Hind II consists of how many base pairs?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'It was found that Hind II always cut DNA molecules at a particular point by recognising a specific sequence of six base pairs.'

questions.text: Q41. Today, more than how many restriction enzymes have been isolated from over how many strains of bacteria?
options: More than 900 restriction enzymes from over 230 strains
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'today we know more than 900 restriction enzymes that have been isolated from over 230 strains of bacteria each of which recognise different recognition sequences.'

questions.text: Q42. In the naming convention of restriction enzymes, the first letter comes from the ________ and the second two letters come from the ________ of the prokaryotic cell.
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'The convention for naming these enzymes is the first letter of the name comes from the genus and the second two letters come from the species of the prokaryotic cell...'

questions.text: Q43. In the restriction enzyme EcoRI, the letter 'R' is derived from:
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5-6: 'e.g., EcoRI comes from Escherichia coli RY 13. In EcoRI, the letter ‘R’ is derived from the name of strain.'

questions.text: Q44. In restriction enzyme nomenclature, the Roman numerals following the names indicate:
options: The order in which the enzymes were isolated from that strain of bacteria
The number of subunits in the enzyme
The base pair length of recognition site
questions.solution: NCERT Page 6: 'Roman numbers following the names indicate the order in which the enzymes were isolated from that strain of bacteria.'

questions.text: Q45. Restriction enzymes belong to a larger class of enzymes called:
questions.solution: NCERT Page 6: 'Restriction enzymes belong to a larger class of enzymes called nucleases. These are of two kinds; exonucleases and endonucleases.'

questions.text: Q46. How do exonucleases differ fundamentally from endonucleases?
options: Exonucleases cut internal phosphodiester bonds, endonucleases remove terminal nucleotides
Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of the DNA, whereas endonucleases make cuts at specific positions within the DNA
Exonucleases act on RNA, endonucleases act on proteins
Exonucleases join sticky ends, endonucleases break hydrogen bonds
questions.solution: NCERT Page 6: 'Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of the DNA whereas, endonucleases make cuts at specific positions within the DNA.'

questions.text: Q47. Each restriction endonuclease functions by 'inspecting' the length of a DNA sequence. Once it finds its specific recognition sequence, it binds and cuts:
options: Each of the two strands of the double helix at specific points in their sugar-phosphate backbones
Only the nitrogenous bases without touching the backbone
questions.solution: NCERT Page 6: 'Once it finds its specific recognition sequence, it will bind to the DNA and cut each of the two strands of the double helix at specific points in their sugar-phosphate backbones (Figure 9.1).'

questions.text: Q48. The chemical bonds cleaved by restriction endonucleases during DNA digestion are:
questions.solution: Restriction endonucleases cut the phosphodiester bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone of both DNA strands (NCERT Page 6).

questions.text: Q49. In Hind II, what do the letters 'H', 'in', and 'd' represent respectively?
questions.solution: Hind II is isolated from bacterium Haemophilus influenzae strain Rd (H = Genus Haemophilus, in = species influenzae, d = strain Rd, II = second enzyme isolated).

questions.text: Q50. Why are restriction enzymes called 'molecular scissors'?
options: Because they cut paper in laboratory tests
Because they cut double-stranded DNA molecules at specific sequence locations
Because they digest unwanted proteins in the cell
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5 refers to restriction enzymes as 'molecular scissors' because of their ability to cut DNA at specific palindromic recognition sequences.

questions.text: Q51. Which of the following is a restriction endonuclease?
questions.solution: EcoRI is a restriction endonuclease. Cellulase, lysozyme, and ribonuclease are cell-wall/RNA degrading enzymes.

questions.text:
Q52. Read the following statements:
Statement I: Exonucleases make cuts at specific positions within the DNA.
Statement II: Endonucleases remove nucleotides from the terminal ends of DNA.
Choose the correct option:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution: Both statements are inverted! NCERT Page 6: Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends, whereas endonucleases make cuts within the DNA.

questions.text: Q53. What protects the host bacterial genome from being degraded by its own restriction endonucleases?
options: Addition of methyl groups to host DNA recognition sites
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5 highlights that in 1963, one enzyme added methyl groups to DNA (modification methylase) to protect host DNA, while the other cut foreign phage DNA.

questions.text: Q54. Bacteriophages are:
questions.solution: Bacteriophages are viruses that parasitize and replicate within bacteria.

questions.text: Q55. The bacterial strain from which EcoRI was originally isolated is:
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5-6: 'e.g., EcoRI comes from Escherichia coli RY 13.'

questions.text: Q56. How many letters from the bacterial species name are included in the standard abbreviation of a restriction enzyme?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'the first letter of the name comes from the genus and the second two letters come from the species...' (e.g. 'co' from coli).

questions.text: Q57. If a restriction enzyme is named BamHI, what does 'H' represent?
questions.solution: In BamHI, B = Bacillus (genus), am = amyloliquefaciens (species), H = strain H, I = first enzyme isolated from this strain.

questions.text: Q58. Which of the following is true regarding the recognition sites of the 900 known restriction enzymes?
options: All 900 recognize the exact same nucleotide sequence
Each of which recognise different recognition sequences
They only act at high temperatures above 100°C
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'isolated from over 230 strains of bacteria each of which recognise different recognition sequences.'

questions.text: Q59. Which property is common to both Hind II and EcoRI?
options: Both are restriction endonucleases that recognize specific palindromic sequences
questions.solution: Both are type II restriction endonucleases recognizing specific palindromic sequences in double-stranded DNA.

questions.text: Q60. The order in which an enzyme was isolated from a given bacterial strain is designated by:
questions.solution: NCERT Page 6: 'Roman numbers following the names indicate the order in which the enzymes were isolated from that strain of bacteria.'

questions.text:
Q61. Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Enzyme Part)
(A) First letter 'E'
(B) Next two letters 'co'
(C) Fourth letter 'R'
(D) Roman numeral 'I'
List-II (Significance in EcoRI)
(I) Species coli
(II) Order of isolation
(III) Genus Escherichia
(IV) Strain RY 13
Choose the correct option:
questions.solution: E = Genus Escherichia (A-III); co = Species coli (B-I); R = Strain RY 13 (C-IV); I = Order of isolation (D-II).

questions.text: Q62. The natural biological role of restriction endonucleases in bacteria is:
questions.solution: Restriction endonucleases function as an adaptive immune defense system in bacteria to restrict and cleave invading bacteriophage genomes.

questions.text: Q63. Restriction endonucleases do NOT cleave:
questions.solution: Restriction endonucleases specifically recognize and cut double-stranded DNA at palindromic sites, not single-stranded mRNA.

questions.text: Q64. If an endonuclease cuts at 5 sites in a circular plasmid DNA, how many fragments will be generated?
questions.solution: Cutting a closed circular DNA at n sites produces exactly n fragments (here, 5 fragments). Cutting a linear DNA at n sites produces n + 1 fragments.

questions.text: Q65. If an endonuclease cuts at 5 sites in a linear DNA molecule, how many fragments will be formed?
questions.solution: In linear DNA, n cuts generate n + 1 fragments. With 5 cuts, 5 + 1 = 6 fragments are generated.

questions.text: Q66. Which of the following describes the inspection mechanism of restriction endonucleases?
options: Inspecting DNA length, binding to specific recognition sequence, and cutting both strands
questions.solution: NCERT Page 6: 'Each restriction endonuclease functions by ‘inspecting’ the length of a DNA sequence. Once it finds its specific recognition sequence, it will bind to the DNA and cut each of the two strands...'

questions.text: Q67. The recognition sequence of a restriction endonuclease is typically characterized by being:
questions.solution: NCERT Page 6: 'Each restriction endonuclease recognises a specific palindromic nucleotide sequences in the DNA.'

questions.text: Q68. The discovery of restriction enzymes was crucial for genetic engineering because:
options: It allowed predictable and reproducible cutting of DNA at precise base sequences
It allowed bacteria to grow without nutrients
questions.solution: Restriction enzymes act as molecular scissors that cut DNA at defined, predictable sites, making the splicing and joining of DNA fragments possible.

questions.text: Q69. Which of the following is an example of an endonuclease that makes a staggered cut creating sticky ends?
questions.solution: EcoRI cuts between G and A in GAATTC, leaving 5'-overhanging sticky ends (NCERT Page 6-7).

questions.text: Q70. The first restriction endonuclease discovered, Hind II, cuts DNA to produce:
questions.solution: Hind II recognizes a 6 bp degenerate sequence (GTPyPuAC) and cuts straight down the middle to produce blunt ends.

questions.text: Q71. In genetics, what is a palindromic sequence of DNA?
options: A sequence that has equal numbers of purines and pyrimidines
A sequence of base pairs that reads same on the two strands when orientation of reading is kept the same (e.g. 5' → 3')
A sequence that codes for stop codons only
A sequence that has only G-C pairs
questions.solution: NCERT Page 6-7: 'the palindrome in DNA is a sequence of base pairs that reads same on the two strands when orientation of reading is kept the same. For example... in 5' → 3' direction.'

questions.text: Q72. Which word is cited in NCERT as a classic example of an English word-palindrome?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 6: 'These are groups of letters that form the same words when read both forward and backward, e.g., “MALAYALAM”.'

questions.text: Q73. What is the exact recognition sequence of EcoRI given in NCERT?
questions.solution:
NCERT Page 6-7: EcoRI recognizes:
5' —— GAATTC —— 3'
3' —— CTTAAG —— 5'

questions.text: Q74. Between which two specific nucleotide bases does EcoRI cut the DNA strands?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 6 (Figure 9.1): 'EcoRI cuts the DNA between bases G and A only when the sequence GAATTC is present in the DNA.'

questions.text: Q75. How does a restriction enzyme generate 'sticky ends'?
options: By cutting straight through the exact center of the palindrome
By cutting a little away from the centre of the palindrome sites, but between the same two bases on opposite strands
questions.solution: NCERT Page 7: 'Restriction enzymes cut the strand of DNA a little away from the centre of the palindrome sites, but between the same two bases on the opposite strands. This leaves single stranded portions at the ends... called sticky ends.'

questions.text: Q76. Why are the single-stranded overhanging stretches called 'sticky ends'?
options: Because they are coated with polysaccharide mucus
Because they form hydrogen bonds with their complementary cut counterparts
Because they adhere to glass tubes permanently
questions.solution: NCERT Page 7: 'These are named so because they form hydrogen bonds with their complementary cut counterparts. This stickiness of the ends facilitates the action of the enzyme DNA ligase.'

questions.text: Q77. The stickiness of overhanging single-stranded ends facilitates the catalytic action of which enzyme?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 7: 'This stickiness of the ends facilitates the action of the enzyme DNA ligase.'

questions.text: Q78. Why must the vector DNA and the source (foreign) DNA be cut with the SAME restriction enzyme in recombinant DNA construction?
options: To ensure they have different base sequences
So that the resultant DNA fragments have complementary matching sticky ends that can pair
questions.solution: NCERT Page 7-8: 'When cut by the same restriction enzyme, the resultant DNA fragments have the same kind of ‘sticky-ends’ and, these can be joined together (end-to-end) using DNA ligases... normally, unless one cuts the vector and the source DNA with the same restriction enzyme, the recombinant vector molecule cannot be created.'

questions.text: Q79. In Figure 9.1 of NCERT, what overhanging sequence is left on the strand when EcoRI cuts 5'-GAATTC-3'?
questions.solution: Cutting between G and A in 5'-G|AATTC-3' leaves a 5'-overhang of AATT on each cut strand (NCERT Page 6, Figure 9.1).

questions.text: Q80. Which type of chemical bond is formed by DNA ligase during joining of recombinant DNA molecules?
questions.solution: While sticky ends anneal by hydrogen bonding, DNA ligase covalently seals the nick by forming phosphodiester bonds between the sugar-phosphate backbones.

questions.text: Q81. A 'recombinant DNA' molecule is defined in NCERT as a molecule composed of DNA from:
options: Different sources / genomes joined together in vitro
questions.solution: NCERT Page 7: 'Restriction endonucleases are used in genetic engineering to form ‘recombinant’ molecules of DNA, which are composed of DNA from different sources/genomes.'

questions.text: Q82. Which of the following DNA sequences is a true palindrome?
questions.solution: Both 5'-GAATTC-3' (EcoRI site) and 5'-ATCGAT-3' (ClaI site) read identically on the opposite strands in 5' → 3' orientation.

questions.text: Q83. In Figure 9.2 (Diagrammatic representation of recombinant DNA technology), what happens immediately after foreign DNA and vector DNA are cut with the same restriction enzyme?
options: Ligases join foreign DNA to plasmid vector
questions.solution: In Figure 9.2 (NCERT Page 7), after restriction cutting, the cut foreign DNA and cut vector are joined by DNA ligase to form the recombinant DNA molecule.

questions.text: Q84. What is the term for introducing the recombinant DNA plasmid into a recipient bacterial cell (e.g. E. coli)?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 7 (Figure 9.2) and Page 9 define transformation as the procedure through which a piece of DNA is introduced into a host bacterium.

questions.text: Q85. If DNA fragments produced by restriction digestion have blunt ends, they:
options: Cannot be joined by any ligase under any condition
questions.solution: Blunt ends are fully base-paired double-stranded termini without overhanging single-stranded stretches.

questions.text: Q86. Which of the following enzymes does NOT create sticky ends?
questions.solution: Hind II produces blunt ends, whereas EcoRI, BamHI, and SalI produce cohesive (sticky) ends.

questions.text: Q87. What facilitates the annealing of sticky ends before DNA ligase seals the phosphodiester backbone?
questions.solution: NCERT Page 7: 'they form hydrogen bonds with their complementary cut counterparts. This stickiness of the ends facilitates the action of the enzyme DNA ligase.'

questions.text: Q88. Can two DNA fragments cut with DIFFERENT restriction enzymes (e.g., EcoRI and BamHI) be efficiently joined together by DNA ligase?
options: Yes, because all restriction enzymes generate identical sticky ends
No, because their sticky ends have non-complementary overhanging sequences
Yes, because DNA ligase does not require base pairing
questions.solution: NCERT Page 8 notes that unless the vector and foreign DNA are cut with the same enzyme, compatible matching sticky ends are not produced, preventing recombinant formation.

questions.text: Q89. The palindrome 5'-GAATTC-3' has how many hydrogen bonds between the complementary base pairs in total?
questions.solution: G-C has 3 H-bonds (2 pairs = 6). A-T has 2 H-bonds (4 pairs = 8). Total H-bonds = 6 + 8 = 14.

questions.text: Q90. In recombinant DNA technology, what acts as the 'glue' that covalently joins DNA fragments?
questions.solution: DNA ligase is often referred to as 'molecular glue' because it joins cut DNA ends by catalyzing phosphodiester bond formation.

questions.text: Q91. Figure 9.1 in NCERT illustrates the action of which specific restriction endonuclease?
questions.solution: NCERT Figure 9.1 is titled: 'Steps in formation of recombinant DNA by action of restriction endonuclease enzyme - EcoRI'.

questions.text: Q92. When foreign DNA is inserted into a cloning vector, the resulting chimeric DNA molecule is called:
questions.solution: NCERT Page 5: 'This makes a new combination of circular autonomously replicating DNA created in vitro and is known as recombinant DNA.'

questions.text: Q93. If the sequence on one strand of DNA is 5' - CTTAAG - 3', what must be the sequence on the opposite strand in 5' → 3' direction to form a palindrome?
questions.solution: By definition, a DNA palindrome reads identically on both strands in the 5' → 3' direction. So the opposite strand in 5' → 3' direction must also be 5' - CTTAAG - 3'.

questions.text: Q94. The staggered cuts made by restriction enzymes leave overhanging stretches on:
options: Each of the cut strands of both vector and foreign DNA
questions.solution: NCERT Page 7: 'There are overhanging stretches called sticky ends on each strand... When cut by the same restriction enzyme, the resultant DNA fragments have the same kind of ‘sticky-ends’...'

questions.text: Q95. Which of the following statements about palindromes in DNA is INCORRECT?
options: They read the same on both strands when reading orientation (e.g. 5' → 3') is kept identical
EcoRI cuts directly between the middle two bases of its palindrome
questions.solution: Statement (C) is INCORRECT because EcoRI cuts 'a little away from the centre of the palindrome sites, but between the same two bases on the opposite strands' (between G and A, not the center!).

questions.text: Q96. The hydrogen bonds that hold annealed sticky ends together are:
options: Relatively weak, non-covalent interactions that temporarily align the ends
questions.solution: Hydrogen bonds are non-covalent bonds that hold base pairs together temporarily until DNA ligase seals the covalent phosphodiester backbone.

questions.text: Q97. In laboratory genetic engineering, DNA ligase is typically sourced from:
questions.solution: T4 DNA ligase (isolated from T4 bacteriophage) is the standard ligase widely used in recombinant DNA technology.

questions.text: Q98. What would happen if foreign DNA and vector DNA were cut with two different enzymes producing non-complementary sticky ends?
options: They cannot easily pair or be joined together to form a recombinant plasmid
Host DNA polymerase would repair the difference instantly
questions.solution: NCERT Page 8: 'normally, unless one cuts the vector and the source DNA with the same restriction enzyme, the recombinant vector molecule cannot be created.'

questions.text: Q99. In Figure 9.2, what is the role of the host cell (such as E. coli)?
options: To act as the cloning host where recombinant plasmid replicates and multiplies
To synthesize restriction endonucleases that degrade foreign DNA
questions.solution: NCERT Figure 9.2 labels E. coli as 'Cloning Host' which divides to produce multiple copies of recombinant DNA.

questions.text: Q100. Which of the following is an obligatory requirement for joining DNA fragments via sticky ends?
questions.solution: All three factors are essential: sequence complementarity for base pairing, DNA ligase for sealing, and ATP as energy cofactor for the ligation reaction.

questions.text: Q101. When a restriction enzyme makes cuts at specific points in the DNA double helix, it cleaves bonds between:
questions.solution: NCERT Page 6: 'cut each of the two strands of the double helix at specific points in their sugar-phosphate backbones.'

questions.text: Q102. Which feature makes sticky ends superior to blunt ends in cloning?
options: Sticky ends require no enzyme at all
Sticky ends facilitate correct directional pairing and much higher ligation efficiency
Sticky ends are completely resistant to all nucleases
questions.solution: Sticky ends spontaneously anneal through complementary base pairing, bringing the 3'-OH and 5'-phosphate termini into close juxtaposition for efficient ligation.

questions.text: Q103. The term 'chimeric DNA' is a synonym for:
questions.solution: Recombinant DNA formed by combining sequences from two different organisms/sources is also referred to as chimeric DNA.

questions.text: Q104. In 5' - GAATTC - 3', how many purine bases are present on the upper strand?
questions.solution: Purines are Adenine (A) and Guanine (G). In G-A-A-T-T-C, G, A, and A are purines (total 3 purines, and T, T, C are 3 pyrimidines).

questions.text: Q105. What is the orientation of reading when verifying a palindromic sequence in double-stranded DNA?
options: 5' → 3' on one strand and 3' → 5' on the same strand
Keeping the same polarity (e.g., 5' → 3' on both strands)
questions.solution: NCERT Page 6-7: 'reads same on the two strands when orientation of reading is kept the same. For example... in 5' → 3' direction. This is also true if read in the 3' → 5' direction.'

questions.text: Q106. In gel electrophoresis, the technique used for separation of DNA fragments is based on which inherent property of DNA molecules?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

DNA fragments are negatively charged molecules because of the phosphate backbone. Therefore, they can be separated by forcing them to move towards the anode (+ve electrode) under an electric field through a medium/matrix.

questions.text: Q107. During agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments move towards which electrode and why?
options: Towards cathode because DNA is positively charged
Towards anode because DNA is negatively charged
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Since DNA fragments are negatively charged, they move towards the positive electrode (anode) under an electric field.

questions.text: Q108. Which is the most commonly used matrix in gel electrophoresis for separating DNA fragments?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Nowadays the most commonly used matrix is agarose, which is a natural polymer extracted from sea weeds.

questions.text: Q109. Agarose, used as a matrix in gel electrophoresis, is extracted from:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Agarose is a natural linear polymer of D-galactose and 3,6-anhydro-L-galactopyranose extracted from sea weeds (marine algae such as Gelidium and Gracilaria).

questions.text: Q110. The separation of DNA fragments on an agarose gel occurs according to their size due to the:
options: Sieving effect provided by the agarose gel
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

The DNA fragments separate (resolve) according to their size through sieving effect provided by the agarose gel. Hence, smaller the fragment size, the farther it moves.

questions.text: Q111. In agarose gel electrophoresis, the smaller the DNA fragment size:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Because of the sieving effect of agarose gel pores, smaller fragments face less resistance and move farther towards the anode compared to larger fragments.

questions.text: Q112. Can the separated DNA fragments on an agarose gel be visualized directly in visible light without staining?
options: No, DNA fragments cannot be seen without staining and UV light
Yes, as bright orange bands under visible light
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

The separated DNA fragments can be visualized only after staining the DNA with a compound known as ethidium bromide followed by exposure to UV radiation (you cannot see pure DNA fragments in the visible light and without staining).

questions.text: Q113. Which chemical compound is used to stain DNA fragments in agarose gel electrophoresis?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Ethidium bromide is an intercalating dye used to stain nucleic acids in agarose gel electrophoresis.

questions.text: Q114. Upon staining with ethidium bromide and exposure to UV radiation, DNA bands appear as:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

You can see bright orange coloured bands of DNA in an ethidium bromide stained gel exposed to UV light.

questions.text: Q115. The process of cutting out separated bands of DNA from the agarose gel and extracting them from the gel piece is known as:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

The separated bands of DNA are cut out from the agarose gel and extracted from the gel piece. This step is known as elution.

questions.text: Q116. Which of the following statements correctly differentiates between 'Spooling' and 'Elution'?
options: Spooling is extraction of DNA from gel; elution is collection of precipitated DNA on a glass rod
Spooling is collection of precipitated DNA on a glass rod; elution is extraction of DNA fragments from agarose gel
Both refer to extraction of DNA from agarose gel
Both refer to precipitation of DNA with chilled ethanol
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Spooling is the mechanical collection of precipitated purified DNA threads onto a glass rod after adding chilled ethanol. Elution is cutting out DNA bands from agarose gel and extracting them.

questions.text: Q117. In a typical agarose gel electrophoresis setup, the sample wells are loaded near which electrode?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Wells are made near the cathode (negative electrode) so that negatively charged DNA fragments migrate across the gel towards the anode (positive electrode).

questions.text: Q118. If four DNA fragments of sizes 10 kb, 5 kb, 2 kb, and 500 bp are separated by agarose gel electrophoresis, which fragment will be found closest to the anode?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (D)

Smaller fragments migrate farther through the sieving matrix towards the anode. 500 bp is the smallest fragment, so it travels fastest and will be closest to the anode.

questions.text: Q119. Which DNA fragment will remain closest to the loading wells after gel electrophoresis?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Larger fragments face maximum resistance through the gel pores and migrate the least distance, thus remaining closest to the loading wells.

questions.text:
Q120. Consider the following statements regarding Gel Electrophoresis:
Statement I: Pure DNA fragments can be seen directly in visible light.
Statement II: DNA fragments are separated based on their charge-to-mass ratio.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Both statements are incorrect. Statement I is false because DNA cannot be seen in visible light without staining. Statement II is false because DNA has a constant charge-to-mass ratio; in agarose gel it separates on the basis of molecular size due to sieving effect.

questions.text: Q121. What is the source of agarose?
options: Red algae (sea weeds like Gelidium and Gracilaria)
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Agarose is extracted from sea weeds, specifically marine red algae such as Gelidium and Gracilaria.

questions.text: Q122. The DNA purified through elution from agarose gel is subsequently used in:
options: Constructing recombinant DNA by joining with cloning vector
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

The DNA fragments purified in this way (elution) are used in constructing recombinant DNA by joining them with the cloning vector.

questions.text: Q123. Why does DNA migrate towards the anode during electrophoresis?
options: Because of the positive charge of purine bases
Because of the negative charge contributed by phosphate groups
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

The phosphate backbone of DNA imparts a net negative charge to the DNA molecule at alkaline pH, causing it to move towards the positive electrode (anode).

questions.text:
Q124. Assertion (A): Smaller DNA fragments travel faster and farther on an agarose gel.
Reason (R): Agarose gel acts as a sieve and provides resistance to the movement of DNA fragments inversely proportional to their size.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

Due to the sieving effect of the gel matrix, smaller molecules pass easily through the pores, while larger molecules face greater hindrance.

questions.text: Q125. What hazardous radiation is required to visualize ethidium bromide-stained DNA bands?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Separated DNA bands stained with ethidium bromide are visualized under ultraviolet (UV) radiation.

questions.text: Q126. Which of the following is NOT a property of agarose?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (C)

Agarose is a natural polysaccharide derived from red sea weeds, not a synthetic polyacrylamide polymer.

questions.text: Q127. In agarose gel electrophoresis, if lane 1 contains uncut plasmid and lane 2 contains plasmid digested with a single-cutting restriction enzyme, what is expected?
options: Lane 2 will show linearized plasmid migrating according to its exact molecular weight
Lane 1 will migrate faster than lane 2 under all conditions
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Digestion with a single-cutting restriction enzyme converts circular plasmid into linear DNA, which migrates as a discrete linear band according to its molecular weight.

questions.text:
Q128. Match Column-I with Column-II regarding Gel Electrophoresis:
A. Agarose — 1. Intercalating dye
B. Ethidium bromide — 2. Natural polymer from sea weeds
C. Elution — 3. Positive electrode
D. Anode — 4. Extraction of DNA from gel piece
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

Agarose is a natural polymer from sea weeds; Ethidium bromide is a fluorescent intercalating dye; Elution is extracting DNA from gel piece; Anode is the positive electrode.

questions.text: Q129. In Figure 9.3 of NCERT showing agarose gel electrophoresis, lane 1 shows:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

In NCERT Figure 9.3, lane 1 shows undigested DNA (a single band near the well), whereas lanes 2 to 4 show digested DNA fragments resolved into multiple bands.

questions.text: Q130. In agarose gel electrophoresis, migration of DNA fragments is influenced by all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Ratio of adenine to thymine alone having varying electrical charges
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (D)

All DNA molecules have uniform negative charge per unit mass regardless of base composition. Thus AT vs GC ratio does not change migration charge.

questions.text: Q131. Why cannot we isolate DNA bands directly under UV light without protective eyewear?
options: UV radiation is mutagenic and harmful to eyes and skin
UV light degrades agarose into toxic gas
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

UV light causes thymine dimers and is carcinogenic/mutagenic, requiring protective eye shields.

questions.text: Q132. Which factor determines the sieving capacity of an agarose gel?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Higher agarose concentration produces smaller pores, suitable for separating smaller DNA fragments, whereas lower concentration allows separation of larger fragments.

questions.text: Q133. During gel electrophoresis, DNA moves through the gel towards the anode because:
options: It is attracted by the hydrophobic gel
It is repelled by the cathode and attracted by the anode due to its negative charge
The buffer flows from cathode to anode by gravity
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

DNA is negatively charged, so under the electrical potential gradient, it is driven from the negative electrode (cathode) towards the positive electrode (anode).

questions.text: Q134. What will happen if an electric current is applied in reverse polarity during gel electrophoresis (anode at the well side)?
options: DNA fragments will run off the gel into the buffer from the wells
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Since DNA is negatively charged, it moves towards the anode. If the anode is behind the wells, DNA will run backwards out of the wells and into the buffer reservoir.

questions.text: Q135. Which statement is INCORRECT regarding Ethidium Bromide?
options: It intercalates between stacked bases of DNA
It fluoresces orange when exposed to UV light
It is completely non-toxic and can be handled without gloves
It is used to stain double-stranded and single-stranded nucleic acids
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (C)

Ethidium bromide is a potent mutagen and potential carcinogen, so it must be handled with extreme care and gloves.

questions.text:
Q136. Statement I: DNA fragments migrate towards the anode during electrophoresis.
Statement II: The smallest DNA fragments move the farthest from the loading wells.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

Both statements are correct. DNA is negatively charged, migrating to the anode, and smaller fragments face less resistance through the agarose matrix, migrating farthest.

questions.text: Q137. In agarose gel electrophoresis, resolution of large DNA fragments (>20 kb) by standard constant voltage electrophoresis is difficult because:
options: Large fragments migrate at nearly the same rate through standard agarose pores (reptation)
Large fragments are destroyed by ethidium bromide
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Standard constant-field electrophoresis cannot resolve very large DNA molecules effectively because they align and snake through pores at similar rates; pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) is needed.

questions.text: Q138. Which part of the nucleotide gives DNA its overall negative charge?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (C)

Each nucleotide has a negatively charged phosphate group at physiological pH, conferring a uniform negative charge density across the DNA chain.

questions.text: Q139. An unknown DNA sample was digested with EcoRI and run on an agarose gel. Three bands were observed. How many EcoRI recognition sites were present in the DNA if it was a linear molecule?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

For a linear DNA molecule, n cleavage sites yield (n + 1) fragments. Since 3 fragments were formed, the number of restriction sites is 3 - 1 = 2.

questions.text: Q140. If a circular plasmid DNA is cut with a restriction enzyme at two restriction sites, how many bands will be seen on an agarose gel?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

For a circular DNA molecule, n cleavage sites yield n fragments. Thus, 2 cutting sites yield 2 fragments.

questions.text: Q141. Which of the following have the ability to replicate within bacterial cells independent of the control of chromosomal DNA?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

Plasmids and bacteriophages have the ability to replicate within bacterial cells independent of the control of chromosomal DNA.

questions.text: Q142. Why do bacteriophages have very high copy numbers of their genome within bacterial cells?
options: Because of their high replication rates independent of host chromosomal control
They depend entirely on host chromosomal division
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Bacteriophages, because of their high number per cell, have very high copy numbers of their genome within bacterial cells.

questions.text: Q143. Plasmids may have a copy number ranging from:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Some plasmids may have only one or two copies per cell whereas others may have 15-100 copies per cell. Their numbers can go even higher.

questions.text: Q144. If an alien piece of DNA is linked with a vector that has a high copy number, the yield of cloned foreign DNA will be:
options: Equal to the copy number of the vector
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (C)

If we are able to link an alien piece of DNA with bacteriophage or plasmid DNA, we can multiply its numbers equal to the copy number of the plasmid or bacteriophage.

questions.text: Q145. Vectors used at present are engineered in such a way that they help in:
options: Easy linking of foreign DNA and selection of recombinants from non-recombinants
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Vectors used at present are engineered in such a way that they help easy linking of foreign DNA and selection of recombinants from non-recombinants.

questions.text: Q146. What is the specific sequence of DNA called where replication is initiated in a vector?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Origin of replication (ori) is a sequence from where replication starts, and any piece of DNA when linked to this sequence can be made to replicate within the host cells.

questions.text: Q147. Which sequence in a cloning vector is responsible for controlling the copy number of the linked alien DNA?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

The origin of replication (ori) is responsible for initiating replication and also controls the copy number of the linked DNA.

questions.text: Q148. If one wants to recover many copies of the target DNA, it should be cloned in a vector whose origin of replication (ori):
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

If one wants to recover many copies of the target DNA, it should be cloned in a vector whose origin supports high copy number.

questions.text: Q149. A 'selectable marker' in a cloning vector helps in:
options: Identifying and eliminating non-transformants and selectively permitting the growth of transformants
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

A selectable marker helps in identifying and eliminating non-transformants and selectively permitting the growth of the transformants.

questions.text: Q150. What is 'transformation' in genetic engineering?
options: The process of translation of mRNA into protein
A procedure through which a piece of DNA is introduced into a host bacterium
Degradation of plasmid DNA by restriction enzymes
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Transformation is a procedure through which a piece of DNA is introduced into a host bacterium.

questions.text: Q151. Under normal conditions, native (non-engineered) Escherichia coli cells carry resistance against which of the following antibiotics?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (D)

Normally, the normal E. coli cells do not carry resistance against any of these antibiotics (ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, or kanamycin).

questions.text: Q152. Which of the following genes are considered useful selectable markers for E. coli vectors?
options: Genes encoding resistance to antibiotics like ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

The genes encoding resistance to antibiotics such as ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin, etc., are considered useful selectable markers for E. coli.

questions.text:
Q153. Assertion (A): Normal E. coli cells are sensitive to ampicillin and tetracycline.
Reason (R): Wild-type E. coli cells do not naturally carry antibiotic resistance genes against ampicillin and tetracycline.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) explains why normal E. coli cells cannot grow on medium containing ampicillin or tetracycline.

questions.text: Q154. What role does a selectable marker play in distinguishing transformants from non-transformants?
options: It confers a trait (e.g. antibiotic resistance) that allows only transformed cells to survive on selective media
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Transformants take up the vector containing the marker (such as an antibiotic resistance gene) and survive on selective antibiotic medium, whereas non-transformants fail to grow and die.

questions.text: Q155. Which of the following is NOT an essential feature of a cloning vector?
options: Presence of human telomeric sequences in bacterial plasmids
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (D)

Essential features of a cloning vector are ori, selectable marker, and cloning site. Human telomeric sequences are only found in linear eukaryotic chromosomes or YACs, not standard bacterial plasmids.

questions.text:
Q156. Statement I: The origin of replication (ori) determines the copy number of the cloned gene.
Statement II: A vector having high copy number ori yields fewer recombinant proteins.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (C)

Statement I is correct because ori controls copy number. Statement II is incorrect because a vector with high copy number yields many copies of the gene and hence higher amounts of recombinant product.

questions.text: Q157. If a foreign DNA is ligated to a vector lacking an 'ori' sequence, what will happen to this DNA in the host cell?
options: It will replicate at a very high rate
It will fail to replicate and will eventually be lost during host cell division
It will integrate into host chromosome automatically
It will transform host into a cancer cell
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Without an origin of replication (ori), DNA replication cannot be initiated, so the alien DNA cannot replicate and will be lost as host cells divide.

questions.text: Q158. Why are bacteriophage vectors often preferred over simple plasmids when cloning large DNA fragments?
options: Bacteriophages can accommodate larger foreign DNA fragments and have high copy numbers
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Bacteriophage vectors can carry larger inserts of foreign DNA and produce a high number of copies per host cell through viral replication.

questions.text: Q159. Selectable markers used in cloning vectors usually encode for:
options: Enzymes that confer resistance to antibiotics or produce color reactions
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Selectable markers typically encode enzymes conferring antibiotic resistance (like beta-lactamase) or chromogenic enzymes (like beta-galactosidase).

questions.text: Q160. In recombinant DNA technology, the term 'Transformant' refers to a bacterial cell that has:
options: Taken up a plasmid or foreign piece of DNA
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

A transformant is a cell that has successfully taken up exogenous DNA (such as a plasmid) through the process of transformation.

questions.text: Q161. What would happen to a culture of non-transformed E. coli cells plated on an agar medium containing ampicillin?
options: They will fail to grow and will not form colonies
They will grow normally and produce ampicillin
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (C)

Since normal E. coli cells lack ampicillin resistance, they are sensitive to ampicillin and will not grow on ampicillin-containing medium.

questions.text: Q162. Which property of plasmids makes them ideal vectors for genetic engineering?
options: Autonomous replication independent of host chromosomal DNA
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Plasmids are extrachromosomal, double-stranded, circular DNA molecules capable of autonomous self-replication independent of the genomic DNA.

questions.text: Q163. The number of plasmid molecules maintained in a single bacterial cell is known as:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

The copy number refers to the average number of copies of a plasmid present per bacterial host cell.

questions.text: Q164. Which of the following antibiotics is NOT typically used as a selectable marker in E. coli vectors?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (C)

Ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, and kanamycin are standard selectable markers for E. coli vectors.

questions.text: Q165. If an alien gene is linked to an ori that supports a copy number of 50, how many copies of the gene are expected per host cell?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (C)

The linked foreign DNA replicates alongside the vector, matching the vector's copy number (50 copies per cell).

questions.text:
Q166. Assertion (A): Plasmids are used as vectors in genetic engineering.
Reason (R): Plasmids have the ability to replicate autonomously within bacterial cells.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

Plasmids make ideal cloning vectors precisely because they replicate autonomously within bacterial cells independent of host chromosome control.

questions.text:
Q167. Match Column-I with Column-II:
A. Ori — 1. Allows selective growth of transformants
B. Selectable marker — 2. Controls copy number of linked DNA
C. Transformation — 3. Extrachromosomal circular autonomous DNA
D. Plasmid — 4. Introduction of foreign DNA into host bacterium
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

Ori controls copy number and starts replication; Selectable marker allows selection of transformants; Transformation is foreign DNA uptake; Plasmid is extrachromosomal circular DNA.

questions.text: Q168. In the development of modern vectors, scientists engineered vectors to have:
options: Multiple origins of replication from different species
Easy linking of foreign DNA and rapid selection of recombinants
No selectable markers to avoid antibiotic use
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Engineered vectors are designed to possess unique cloning sites for easy insertion and reliable selectable markers for differentiating recombinants from non-recombinants.

questions.text: Q169. What prevents a plasmid without an 'ori' from being maintained in a bacterial population over multiple generations?
options: It cannot replicate during cell division and is diluted out in daughter cells
It prevents transcription of all bacterial genes
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Without an ori, the plasmid cannot duplicate when the bacterial cell divides. Consequently, only one daughter cell inherits it initially, and it quickly dilutes out.

questions.text: Q170. Which antibiotic resistance gene in pBR322 confers resistance against ampicillin?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

The amp^R gene confers resistance to the antibiotic ampicillin by encoding beta-lactamase.

questions.text: Q171. Which antibiotic resistance gene in pBR322 confers resistance against tetracycline?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

The tet^R gene encodes proteins conferring resistance against tetracycline.

questions.text: Q172. When a recipient bacterium takes up naked DNA from the surrounding environment, the phenomenon is called:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (C)

Transformation is the process by which a competent bacterial cell takes up exogenous naked DNA from its surrounding medium.

questions.text: Q173. Why are antibiotic resistance genes essential components of artificial plasmid vectors?
options: They supply nutrients to the host bacterium
They ensure that only bacteria containing the plasmid grow in the presence of the antibiotic
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

They act as selectable markers so researchers can kill untransformed bacteria by adding the antibiotic, leaving only transformed cells.

questions.text:
Q174. Consider the following statements:
Statement I: Plasmids are double-stranded circular DNA molecules.
Statement II: Bacteriophages always have lower copy numbers than plasmids.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (C)

Statement I is correct. Statement II is incorrect because bacteriophages typically have very high copy numbers per cell, often exceeding typical low-copy plasmids.

questions.text: Q175. A researcher wishes to clone a human gene and obtain high yields of the gene product. Which vector feature is most critical to select?
options: A vector with a low copy number ori
A vector with an ori supporting high copy number
A vector with multiple restriction sites for the same enzyme
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

To obtain high yields of the cloned gene and its product, a vector with an origin of replication supporting a high copy number is preferred.

questions.text: Q176. Why should a cloning vector preferably have only a single recognition site for a commonly used restriction enzyme?
options: Because presence of more than one recognition site will generate several fragments, complicating gene cloning
To allow multiple genes to insert simultaneously
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

In order to link the alien DNA, the vector needs to have very few, preferably single, recognition sites for the commonly used restriction enzymes. Presence of more than one recognition site within the vector will generate several fragments, which will complicate the gene cloning.

questions.text: Q177. In the diagram of vector pBR322 (NCERT Figure 9.4), what does 'p', 'BR', and '322' stand for?
options: p = protein, BR = Boyer & RFLP, 322 = page number
p = plasmid, BR = Bolivar and Rodriguez, 322 = order/strain number
p = promoter, BR = Bacteria & Recombinant, 322 = base pairs
p = phage, BR = Brown & Robert, 322 = molecular weight
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

In pBR322: 'p' denotes plasmid; 'BR' honors the scientists Francisco Bolivar and Raymond Rodriguez who constructed it; '322' is the laboratory numerical designation distinguishing it from other plasmids.

questions.text: Q178. Which restriction endonuclease recognition sites are located within the ampicillin resistance (amp^R) gene of pBR322?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

In pBR322, the recognition sites for PvuI and PstI are located within the amp^R (ampicillin resistance) gene.

questions.text: Q179. Which restriction endonuclease recognition sites are located within the tetracycline resistance (tet^R) gene of pBR322?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

In pBR322, the recognition sites for BamHI and SalI are present within the tet^R (tetracycline resistance) gene.

questions.text: Q180. What does the 'rop' gene in pBR322 code for?
options: Proteins involved in the replication of the plasmid
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

The 'rop' gene codes for the proteins involved in the replication of the plasmid (Repressor of Primer).

questions.text: Q181. Which restriction endonuclease recognition site is located within the 'rop' region of pBR322?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

The restriction site PvuII is located within the rop region of pBR322.

questions.text: Q182. Which of the following restriction sites are present in pBR322 outside the antibiotic resistance genes and rop?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

In pBR322, the recognition sites for EcoRI, ClaI, and HindIII are located in the region adjacent to each other, outside the amp^R and tet^R genes.

questions.text: Q183. If a foreign DNA is ligated at the BamHI site of vector pBR322, the recombinant plasmid will:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Ligation of alien DNA at the BamHI site of the tet^R gene causes insertional inactivation of the tetracycline resistance gene. Therefore, the recombinant plasmid loses tetracycline resistance while retaining ampicillin resistance.

questions.text: Q184. The phenomenon where insertion of a recombinant DNA within the coding sequence of a gene causes it to become non-functional is called:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

Insertional inactivation is the inactivation of a gene due to the insertion of foreign DNA within its coding sequence.

questions.text: Q185. Recombinant E. coli cells carrying pBR322 with a foreign gene inserted at the BamHI site will grow on:
options: Ampicillin medium but not on tetracycline medium
Tetracycline medium but not on ampicillin medium
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

Because of insertional inactivation of the tet^R gene at the BamHI site, the recombinants will grow on ampicillin-containing medium but not on medium containing tetracycline.

questions.text: Q186. Non-recombinant E. coli transformants carrying intact pBR322 (no foreign insert) will grow on:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (C)

Non-recombinant transformants retain both functional amp^R and tet^R genes, so they will grow on both ampicillin-containing and tetracycline-containing media.

questions.text: Q187. To select recombinants from non-recombinants using pBR322 with an insert at BamHI site, the transformants are first plated on:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Transformants are first plated on ampicillin-containing medium to allow all transformants (both recombinants and non-recombinants) to grow, while non-transformants die.

questions.text: Q188. Following growth on ampicillin medium, how are the colonies tested for tetracycline sensitivity?
options: By PCR amplification of all colonies simultaneously
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

The transformants growing on ampicillin-containing medium are then transferred (replica plated) onto a medium containing tetracycline.

questions.text: Q189. Colonies that grow on ampicillin plate but FAIL to grow when replica-plated onto tetracycline plate are:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (C)

Recombinants grow on ampicillin (intact amp^R) but fail to grow on tetracycline due to insertional inactivation of tet^R at the BamHI site.

questions.text: Q190. Why is selection of recombinants using antibiotic resistance genes considered a cumbersome procedure?
options: It requires simultaneous plating on two plates having different antibiotics
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Selection of recombinants due to inactivation of antibiotics is a cumbersome procedure because it requires simultaneous plating on two plates having different antibiotics (replica plating).

questions.text: Q191. What alternative selectable marker has been developed to differentiate recombinants on the basis of colour production?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Alternative selectable markers have been developed which differentiate recombinants from non-recombinants on the basis of their ability to produce colour in the presence of a chromogenic substrate, using the gene for enzyme beta-galactosidase.

questions.text: Q192. In chromogenic selection with beta-galactosidase, what happens when a recombinant DNA is inserted into the coding sequence of the enzyme?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

A recombinant DNA is inserted within the coding sequence of an enzyme, beta-galactosidase. This results into inactivation of the gene for synthesis of this enzyme, which is referred to as insertional inactivation.

questions.text: Q193. In the presence of a chromogenic substrate (such as X-gal), bacterial colonies containing non-recombinant plasmids will appear:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

If the plasmid in the bacterium does not have an insert (non-recombinant), the beta-galactosidase gene is intact and active, giving blue coloured colonies in the presence of a chromogenic substrate.

questions.text: Q194. In the presence of a chromogenic substrate, colonies formed by recombinant bacteria (with insertional inactivation of beta-galactosidase) appear:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Presence of insert results into insertional inactivation of the beta-galactosidase gene and the colonies do not produce any colour; these are identified as recombinant colonies (white colonies).

questions.text: Q195. What is the major advantage of using beta-galactosidase insertional inactivation (blue-white selection) over antibiotic replica plating?
options: It requires two sets of antibiotic plates
Recombinants are identified directly in a single step based on colony color without replica plating
Blue colonies are recombinant and faster to harvest
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Blue-white screening eliminates the tedious step of dual antibiotic replica plating; recombinant white colonies can be picked directly from a single primary transformation plate.

questions.text: Q196. If a foreign DNA fragment is inserted into the PstI site of pBR322, the recombinant plasmid will confer resistance to:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

The PstI site is located within the amp^R gene. Inserting foreign DNA here disrupts amp^R, making the recombinant sensitive to ampicillin but remaining resistant to tetracycline.

questions.text: Q197. If foreign DNA is ligated at the SalI site of pBR322, the transformants that grow on ampicillin but die on tetracycline are:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

SalI is located in the tet^R gene. Disruption by insertion causes loss of tetracycline resistance while ampicillin resistance remains intact; these are recombinant transformants.

questions.text:
Q198. Assertion (A): Presence of more than one recognition site for a restriction enzyme within a cloning vector is undesirable.
Reason (R): More than one recognition site generates several fragments, which complicates gene cloning.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

Having multiple recognition sites for the same enzyme cuts the vector into many pieces, preventing predictable circularization and complicating cloning.

questions.text: Q199. How many recognition sites for the enzyme EcoRI are present in the cloning vector pBR322?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

pBR322 has exactly one unique recognition site for EcoRI (as well as for ClaI, HindIII, BamHI, SalI, PvuI, PstI, and PvuII).

questions.text:
Q200. Match the restriction endonuclease with its location in plasmid pBR322:
A. PvuI — 1. tet^R gene
B. BamHI — 2. amp^R gene
C. PvuII — 3. Outside antibiotic genes
D. EcoRI — 4. rop gene
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

PvuI is in amp^R; BamHI is in tet^R; PvuII is in rop; EcoRI is outside the antibiotic resistance genes.

questions.text: Q201. In blue-white selection, what is the chromogenic substrate commonly used to detect beta-galactosidase activity?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

X-gal is a chromogenic substrate cleaved by active beta-galactosidase to produce an insoluble blue product (5,5'-dibromo-4,4'-dichloro-indigo).

questions.text: Q202. A plasmid pBR322 was digested with ClaI and ligated with a foreign DNA cut with ClaI. How will you select the recombinant bacteria?
options: By their ability to grow on ampicillin and failure to grow on tetracycline
ClaI does not interrupt either amp^R or tet^R, so both resistances are retained
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

The ClaI site in pBR322 lies outside both amp^R and tet^R genes. Therefore, insertion at ClaI does not cause insertional inactivation of either antibiotic gene; recombinants remain resistant to both ampicillin and tetracycline.

questions.text:
Q203. Statement I: In pBR322, the rop gene codes for the repressor of primer proteins that regulate plasmid replication.
Statement II: Disruption of the rop gene leads to complete loss of plasmid replication.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (C)

Statement I is correct. Statement II is incorrect because rop regulates (restrains) copy number; deleting or disrupting rop typically causes an increase in plasmid copy number rather than abolishing replication.

questions.text: Q204. In pBR322, if foreign DNA is inserted at the PvuII site, which of the following is inactivated?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (C)

The PvuII recognition site is located within the rop gene. Inserting DNA at this site causes insertional inactivation of rop.

questions.text: Q205. Which of the following bacteria is the source organism of plasmid pBR322?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Plasmid pBR322 was engineered by Francisco Bolivar and Raymond Rodriguez using genetic elements from Escherichia coli plasmids.

questions.text:
Q206. Consider the following outcomes in a transformation experiment with pBR322 (foreign gene inserted at BamHI site):
1. Sensitive to both ampicillin and tetracycline
2. Resistant to ampicillin but sensitive to tetracycline
3. Resistant to both ampicillin and tetracycline
Identify: Non-transformant, Recombinant transformant, and Non-recombinant transformant respectively.
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

1 = Non-transformant (lacks pBR322, killed by both drugs); 2 = Recombinant (amp^R intact, tet^R disrupted); 3 = Non-recombinant (both amp^R and tet^R intact).

questions.text: Q207. In blue-white selection, why do recombinant colonies appear white?
options: Insertional inactivation of the beta-galactosidase gene prevents cleavage of the chromogenic substrate
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Foreign DNA insertion interrupts the lacZ coding sequence, producing an inactive beta-galactosidase that cannot hydrolyze X-gal, leaving the colonies uncoloured (white).

questions.text: Q208. Which feature in a cloning vector is illustrated by the site 'ori' in Figure 9.4?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (A)

'ori' stands for origin of replication, the sequence where replication of plasmid DNA begins.

questions.text: Q209. If you want to clone a gene into pBR322 and use insertional inactivation of the ampicillin resistance gene, which restriction enzyme would you choose?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (C)

PstI (or PvuI) cuts within the amp^R gene. Inserting DNA here inactivates ampicillin resistance.

questions.text: Q210. What is the phenotypic characteristic of untransformed E. coli when plated on nutrient agar containing tetracycline?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (C)

Untransformed E. coli lacks resistance genes and is killed by tetracycline, forming no colonies.

questions.text: Q211. Which bacterium is known as 'natural genetic engineer' of plants?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Agrobacterium tumefaciens, a pathogen of several dicot plants, is known as nature's genetic engineer because it naturally transfers a piece of DNA (T-DNA) to transform normal plant cells into tumor cells.

questions.text: Q212. Agrobacterium tumefaciens infects which group of plants naturally?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Agrobacterium tumefaciens is a pathogen of several dicot plants.

questions.text: Q213. What is the piece of DNA called that Agrobacterium tumefaciens transfers into plant cells to induce tumors?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Agrobacterium tumefaciens delivers a piece of DNA known as 'T-DNA' to transform normal plant cells into a tumor.

questions.text: Q214. The tumor-inducing plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens is called:
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

The tumor inducing (Ti) plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens has been modified into a cloning vector.

questions.text: Q215. What makes the modified Ti plasmid safe and useful as a vector for cloning genes into higher plants?
options: It has been disarmed and is no longer pathogenic to plants
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

The tumor inducing (Ti) plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens has now been modified (disarmed) so that it is no longer pathogenic to the plants but is still able to use the mechanisms to deliver genes of our interest into a variety of plants.

questions.text: Q216. How have retroviruses in animals been harnessed for genetic engineering?
options: By allowing them to cause cancer in animals
By disarming them and using them to deliver desirable genes into animal cells
questions.solution:
Correct Answer: (B)

Retroviruses in animals have the ability to transform normal cells into cancerous cells. Similarly, retroviruses have been disarmed and are now used to deliver desirable genes into animal cells.
